topic: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem: Fairness in a Necklace

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Intuition of Antipodes
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a sphere (S²) and antipodal points—pairs of points exactly opposite each other on the surface. Visualize this as the North and South poles, or any point (x, y, z) and its reflection (-x, -y, -z).
sections.example: An animation showing a globe where if you touch a spot in Tokyo, the antipodal point is deep in the Atlantic Ocean near Argentina.

sections.title: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem (The Core Concept)
sections.content: State the theorem: Any continuous function from an n-sphere to n-dimensional Euclidean space must map at least one pair of antipodal points to the same value. Use the 'Temperature/Pressure' analogy: there exist two opposite points on Earth with identical temperature and pressure.
sections.example: Visualizing a 2D map of Earth where two 'thermometers' are linked by a rigid bar; as you rotate the bar, they eventually hit two points of identical temperature.

sections.title: Transition: From Spheres to Necklaces
sections.content: Explain how the 'Stolen Necklace Problem' is a discrete combinatorial application of this topological theorem. We have a necklace with beads of different types (e.g., gold and silver) and need to cut it into pieces to distribute fairly among two thieves.
sections.example: Two thieves, Alice and Bob, have a string of 10 gold beads and 10 silver beads. They want to cut the string so both get exactly 5 gold and 5 silver beads.

sections.title: Application: Solving the Necklace Problem
sections.content: Demonstrate the theorem's power: If there are 'k' types of beads, the necklace can be split fairly using at most 'k' cuts. This transforms a complex search problem into a topological existence proof.
sections.example: An animation of a 2-colored necklace. As a slider moves, the necklace 'deforms' into a shape that satisfies the Borsuk-Ulam requirements, showing exactly where the cuts must be made to ensure an equal split.

sections.title: Conclusion: Why Symmetry Matters
sections.content: Summarize that Borsuk-Ulam is a 'fixed-point' style theorem that guarantees fairness in distributed systems. It shows that in any sufficiently complex system, perfect balance (symmetry) is not just possible—it is mathematically inevitable.
sections.example: A final visual showing the 'perfectly cut' necklace distributed between two animated characters, emphasizing that math provided the 'fair judge'.
